sentences.text: The barley on the north side of the road had been ploughed in the second week of March.
That is the whole explanation and it took Rocío four days and one telephone call to establish it.
The field had changed hands in the winter.
The new man was from Valladolid and was perfectly reasonable and was farming it in the ordinary modern way, which meant the whole field, up to the road, in one pass.
Larks nest on the ground.

They need a strip of rough where nothing runs a machine over them between April and July, and if there is no strip there is no nest, and if there is no nest there is no bird going up before light and hanging there for an hour and forty minutes over a village that had built its entire morning underneath her.
Rocío has since read enough to know that this is one of the best-documented declines in Europe and that Fuentelosa's version of it was not special in any way.
The birds have gone from most of that country for exactly this reason and there are papers about it and there is nothing supernatural in a single line of the mechanism.
What was special about Fuentelosa is only that somebody was counting.
Rocío was twelve and she took this to her grandmother, who took it to the wall by the fountain.
It was not a meeting and there was no vote.

What there was, over about nine days, was a conversation that happened in the bread queue in the fifty minutes it had left, and at the end of the nine days three farmers on the north side of that road had each agreed to leave four metres unploughed along the top edge, which between them made a strip about six hundred metres long.
The man from Valladolid was one of the three and Rocío would like that recorded, because when she tells this story people always want him to be the villain and he was not.
He asked what it was for.
He was told, by her grandmother, in about two sentences, in a bread queue.
He said all right.
Rocío asked her grandmother afterwards what the two sentences had been.
Her grandmother could not remember and did not consider it interesting.
What Rocío thinks now, having spent twenty years in meetings, is that this is the part of the story nobody believes and the part most worth attending to.
There was no campaign.
Nobody wrote to anybody.
Six hundred metres of a working field came out of production because an old woman said something to a man in a queue and he had no particular reason to say no.
There was a lark the following spring.
There has been one every spring since.
Rocío is thirty-four.
She works in Palencia and drives back at weekends, and Fuentelosa now has forty-one people in it and the school shut in 2016.
The bread queue is six people and it lasts about twenty minutes and there are two men on the wall.
But the morning is still an hour and forty minutes long, and on Saturdays Rocío gets up in the dark for no reason she can defend, and stands in the road, and waits for it to start.
